The sequence

Research in the right order.

1

Define the guest

Know the trip, party size and booking trigger before choosing a ZIP code.

2

Map demand drivers

Look for several reasons to visit across different seasons—not one fragile attraction.

3

Clear the rule stack

Confirm state, county, city, HOA, deed, tax, insurance and safety obligations in writing.

4

Zoom into the neighborhood

Test drive times, road access, noise, views, walkability and guest friction.

5

Underwrite the ordinary year

Use conservative occupancy, seasonal rates and a real reserve for operating surprises.

Market-selection workbook

Move from a promising city to an address you can defend

A market thesis should survive four levels of scrutiny: the region attracts real trips, the jurisdiction permits the intended use, the neighborhood matches the guest, and the property can deliver the stay profitably. This expanded workbook adds the evidence, red flags, and decision gates that turn a watchlist into a disciplined buy box.

Best for: short-term-rental buyers comparing markets before they commit to a property search.

Keep the analysis honest. Rules, taxes, insurance, and booking patterns change. Treat every market note as a research starting point and verify current requirements with authoritative local sources.

Eight decisions to work through

Define the trip

Identify why guests come, who travels, typical party size, booking window, length of stay, and the substitute destinations they consider.

Put it to work: Build the guest thesis before studying revenue estimates.

Separate durable and event demand

Universities, hospitals, employment, recreation, family travel, and events create different calendars and recession behavior.

Put it to work: Map several independent demand drivers across all twelve months.

Trace the complete rule stack

State law, county rules, municipal codes, zoning, permits, taxes, HOA documents, deeds, lenders, and insurers may all matter.

Put it to work: Save dated source links and written confirmations for the exact parcel.

Zoom to the micro-location

Drive time, road quality, noise, safety, views, walkability, parking, and proximity can change performance within one ZIP code.

Put it to work: Compare guest reviews and map friction at the neighborhood level.

Build a property-specific comp set

Match bedroom count, capacity, amenity tier, location, quality, and availability rather than relying on market-wide averages.

Put it to work: Exclude listings that are not true substitutes for the planned guest.

Model an ordinary year

Use seasonal rates, realistic occupancy, ramp-up, fees, cancellations, cleaning, utilities, repairs, management, and reserves.

Put it to work: Stress-test rate and occupancy together because weak periods often affect both.

Match operations to distance

Remote markets add vendor, maintenance, inspection, weather, supply, and emergency-response dependencies.

Put it to work: Confirm local coverage before assigning a value to passive management.

Set decision gates

A good search has explicit reasons to advance, pause, or reject a market before excitement attaches to a listing.

Put it to work: Score evidence quality as well as the market itself.

Questions readers ask before they act

What makes a demand driver durable?

Repeated travel need, diversified visitor reasons, broad seasonality, and evidence that does not depend on one venue or temporary trend.

How current must regulatory research be?

Current enough to support today’s address-specific decision; verify again before contract, before closing, and before operating.

Are revenue tools sufficient?

No. They are inputs that require a good comp set, local context, property adjustments, and conservative cost assumptions.

How should seasonality be handled?

Model monthly revenue and cash needs so annual averages do not hide long low-season stretches or working-capital strain.

What is a strong fallback?

A legal and economically plausible alternate rental or resale use that does not require heroic renovation or market timing.

When is a market ready for property search?

When the guest, rules, neighborhoods, operating model, cost structure, downside, and decision criteria are documented.
